source: Terminology class notes: Terminology, Week 1 [Shaikhah Alkhaledi]

rows.item: Discussion questions: what “terminology” brings to mind; terminology versus semantics and lexicography; examples of specialised terminologies
rows.note: Class discussion prompts, not teaching content.

rows.item: Introduction: no agreement on what terminology is; it borrowed from semantics, lexicology and lexicography
rows.note: Theory about the field itself; too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Beginnings of modern terminology: advances in science and technology (genetics, space exploration, information science, telecommunications); contact between language communities; divergent views (standardising, technical lexicography, word lists)
rows.note: History and theory; too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Meanings of terminology: the technical terms of an art, science or subject, and later the study of those terms
rows.note: Chapter 21 has its own short entries for “Terminology” in Words to remember, so the history of the word was not needed.

rows.item: The long definition of terminology as a discipline (identifying, analysing, creating and standardising terms) and the four work methods (term identification, contextual analysis, term creation, standardisation)
rows.note: Too theoretical; the handbook gives a one-line definition of terminology from another source and teaches the practical steps in Chapter 21 instead.

rows.item: Term identification: simple terms, complex terms (two or more words for one concept) and phrases
rows.note: Only the idea that a term can be several words is kept; simple terms and phrases were left out.

rows.item: Contextual analysis: finding a term’s meaning by delimiting its context and pinpointing semantic features
rows.note: Too technical; the handbook keeps only the simple point that the context decides (Chapter 21, Step 3).

rows.item: Term creation: gaps between languages; the terminologist identifies existing terms and coins one only after all sources have been searched
rows.note: Kept in the handbook’s own words as ‘search for an accepted term first; create one only if none exists’; the point about gaps between languages is not stated separately.

rows.item: Standardisation: research and standardisation go together; less arbitrary decisions on usage
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

source: Terminology class notes: Terminology 2, Week 2 [Shaikhah Alkhaledi]

rows.item: Specialised terms: each field (arts, science, business, economics, law, medicine) has its own special language; a special language holds general words and terms; terminology studies terms, not general vocabulary
rows.note: Chapter 21 opens with its own beginner explanation of terms, using contract and medical leaflet examples.

rows.item: Definitions and contexts: terminologists check current usage; situational context versus written context; semantic features
rows.note: Too technical; Chapter 7 teaches how context decides meaning in simpler terms.

rows.item: Bilingual terminology: finding enough information on the source term in context to research the target equivalent (textual correspondence)
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: The user’s need for means of expression: an advertiser’s needs differ from a scientist’s; users need to know what something is called
rows.note: Background theory; not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: Terminology records: manual records replaced by computerised databases
rows.note: Record formats are too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Terminological media: databases (multiple access, fast retrieval); vocabularies (alphabetical; source entry, target equivalent, short definition, subfield); glossaries; teaching outlines and illustrations
rows.note: Chapter 21, Step 4 shows a simple term list instead.

rows.item: Exercises: find simple terms, complex terms and phrases in a short text and set them out as a vocabulary; general language versus special languages; vocabulary versus terminology
rows.note: Class exercises; the handbook has its own Try it questions.

source: Terminology class notes: Term and Concept, Week 5 [Shaikhah Alkhaledi]

rows.item: Term and concept: the signifier (the word) and the signified (the object), linked through concepts in the mind
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: What is a term: a word or expression that designates a concept of a subject field; simple, complex or phrase
rows.note: Chapter 21 has its own one-line entry for “Term” in Words to remember.

rows.item: Simple terms: coproduce, commentator, monochrome, and why their affixes do not make them complex
rows.note: Too technical for beginners.

rows.item: Complex terms: captive audience, laughmeter, director-producer, closeup, ultrawide-angle lens, to lip sync; one concept, and removing a word changes the concept
rows.note: Only the idea is kept (several words, one idea, translate as one unit), with the example network security; the television examples were not used.

rows.item: Phrasal terms: request for copyright clearance, to preempt a program, filmed on location, on the air
rows.note: Too technical for beginners.

rows.item: Concept and essential characteristics: the concept watch (face and hands, tells time, worn on a wristband)
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: Specificity to subject field: general words given new meanings (street furniture, information highway)
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: One term in several fields: carrier in telecommunication, transportation, insurance and medicine; strictly, a term belongs to one field
rows.note: Only the idea is used (one word is a different term in each field), shown with the depression example instead of carrier.

rows.item: Objects: material and immaterial; classes (entities, properties, activities, dimensions)
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: The link between term and concept is arbitrary and based on convention
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: Motivation: films library, catwalk, soap opera; motivation is useful but not necessary (blackboard can be green); desirable in new terms
rows.note: Only blackboard is kept, to show that a term’s parts can mislead and the context decides.

rows.item: Classification of concepts: generic and partitive relations (sampling, bicycle); causal and opposite relations (biased sampling, systematic versus unsystematic)
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: Exercise: list five motivated terms in a subject and explain why they are motivated
rows.note: Class exercise; the handbook has its own Try it questions.

source: Terminology class notes: Definitions in Terminology, Week 10 [Shaikhah Alkhaledi]

rows.item: Purpose of a terminological definition: the essential characteristics only; different from dictionary and encyclopedia definitions
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: Rules of definition: not obscure; not too broad or too narrow; able to replace the term
rows.note: Too advanced; the handbook gives one simple rule for definitions instead.

rows.item: Rules of definition: not circular (herpetologist); not negative where a positive is possible (chair; exceptions undifferentiated, achromatic)
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Definition by genus and difference: name the larger class, then what sets the concept apart (man as a rational animal)
rows.note: Kept as a plain rule (name the general group, then say what makes the term different); the example is the handbook’s own, thermometer.

rows.item: Other methods: partition definition, definition by description (mirror), operational definition (product), synonymous definition (bellis perennis as daisy)
rows.note: Too advanced; one method is enough for a beginner.

rows.item: Choice of method: evening dress by partition; cake by genus, parts or recipe
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Choice of defining words: nouns (techno-casualty, audiodontics), verbs (airdash, auralize), adjectives (congenial, ageist, disinformative, proactive, back-of-the-book), adverbs (hyperacutely, utopianly)
rows.note: Grammar detail that is too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Good practice: adequacy, brevity (no longer than one sentence or phrase) and clarity
rows.note: Only brevity is kept: write the definition in one sentence.

source: Terminology class notes: Term Formation and Standardization, Week 10 [Shaikhah Alkhaledi]

rows.item: Introduction: terms are rarely invented from nothing; they come from new meanings, changed form or word class, and borrowing
rows.note: Chapter 17 teaches ways to make Arabic words instead.

rows.item: Term formation in different fields: classical derivation in biology, borrowing in earth sciences, little borrowing in computer science
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: Features of English term formation: productive; compounds and metaphor; borrowing from Latin, Greek, French and German
rows.note: These are about English; the handbook’s concern is Arabic.

rows.item: Reasons for creating terms: innovation, changing attitudes, social change (policewoman, chairwoman, businesswoman), effective communication (telephone network)
rows.note: Chapter 17, Step 1 gives the beginner reason for new words instead (gaps in the target language).

rows.item: Four processes of English term formation: semantic change, morphological change, conversion, borrowing
rows.note: Too technical; Chapter 17 gives five ways to make Arabic words.

rows.item: General rules of term formation: concision, linguistic accuracy, motivation, monosemy, ability to produce derivatives
rows.note: The handbook has its own one-sentence rule for a good term in Chapter 21, Step 3.

rows.item: Who forms terms: inventors, and terminologists working with specialists
rows.note: Not needed at beginner level.

rows.item: Standardisation: consensus, expert committees, synonyms in different regions, and why it is triggered
rows.note: Too advanced; Chapter 21, Step 2 says only that the Arabic language academies create and approve terms.

source: Terminology class notes: Subject Field Research, Week 5 [Shaikhah Alkhaledi]

rows.item: Introduction: subject-field research is exhaustive and slow; six preliminary stages before scanning for terms
rows.note: Research on a whole field is too advanced; the handbook works term by term.

rows.item: Stage 1, determining objectives with the client: purpose, target audience, scope (a few hundred or a few thousand concepts)
rows.note: Chapter 2 asks three questions (client, purpose, audience) for a single translation instead.

rows.item: Stage 2, estimating resources: staff, money, and documents, glossaries, bibliographic databases and term banks
rows.note: Project planning is too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Documentary resources: original documents in the source and target languages, not translations
rows.note: Kept as advice to confirm the equivalent in a text written in Arabic by specialists, not in a translation.

rows.item: Stage 3, becoming familiar with the field: read a short work for beginners; introductory textbooks and encyclopedia entries
rows.note: Kept as: if the field is new, read a short introduction first, such as an encyclopedia entry.

rows.item: Stage 4, selecting documentation: quality over quantity; three or four works plus a specialised dictionary; six to eight in the target language
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Stage 5, locating documentation: textbooks, handbooks, national standards (CSA, ASTM), librarians and specialists
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Stage 6, evaluating documentation: table of contents, index, quality of writing, author’s credibility
rows.note: Too advanced; Chapter 3, Step 2 asks readers to check a dictionary’s publisher instead.

rows.item: Breakdown of the subject field into subfields and related fields
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Scanning for terms: each term must fit the breakdown; better to include too many at first
rows.note: Chapter 2 asks readers to list the key terms of a text instead.

source: Terminology class notes: Terminology, Semantics and Lexicography, Week 3 [Shaikhah Alkhaledi]

rows.item: Introduction: terminology is often confused with other disciplines; it is independent
rows.note: Theory about the field itself; too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Semantics: sign and referent; the historical approach (fish from Old English fisc; later meanings flesh, a mast piece, a cold person) and the descriptive approach (polysemy, semantic range)
rows.note: Too theoretical; Chapter 7 teaches polysemy with its own examples.

rows.item: Terminology begins with context, not etymology (fish in biology)
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: How terminology relates to semantics, and how semantic change (analogy, metonymy) forms terms
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: Terminology and lexicography: the whole lexicon versus a specialised stock; concept to sign versus sign to concept; encoding versus decoding
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: Work methods compared: nomenclature, term identification, analysis, definition
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Key information media: dictionary entry versus terminology record (one concept, tied to its context, an encoding tool)
rows.note: Record formats are too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: End products: the dictionary versus a growing file of terminology records
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Exercises: study bank, charge, mouse, virus, tank and cell as lexicographer and as terminologist; compare the two methods
rows.note: Class exercises; Chapter 7 uses other examples of words with several meanings.

source: Terminology class notes: The Situation in Terminology, Week 3 [Shaikhah Alkhaledi]

rows.item: Terminology has a social function; one concept has different labels in different situations (total impacts / gross audience)
rows.note: The advertising example was not needed; the aerial and antenna example was used instead (next item).

rows.item: One concept, two labels by place: aerial in England, antenna in the United States
rows.note: Kept as an example of a concept with two accepted names; the handbook added the Arabic {{هوائي}} and a second pair, {{حاسوب}} and {{كمبيوتر}}.

rows.item: The situational context comes first; the Palmer quotation on living languages; terminology cannot be built outside context
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: Situation and view of reality: each language sees the world differently, which affects equivalence
rows.note: Too theoretical for beginners.

rows.item: Comparative terminology: terms are not literal translations (whistleblower, goalkeeper, {{مجلات علمية}}); living terminology is idiomatic
rows.note: Chapter 11 already shows that word-for-word translation often fails.

rows.item: Problems of living terminology: synonyms, several meanings, obscure wording; describing usage versus choosing it
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: The role of users: they help researchers; terminologists provide tools, not protection of terms
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Work methods: a real need, target audience, level of language, data gathering, signs and labels, selecting terms
rows.note: Chapter 2 asks about client, purpose and audience for a translation instead.

rows.item: Situation and standardisation: describing usage versus prescribing it; the two are complementary
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

source: Terminology class notes: Term Research, Week 5 [Shaikhah Alkhaledi]

rows.item: Introduction and advantages: term research answers questions on single terms; it trains novices; clients need answers in 4 to 48 hours
rows.note: Describes the terminologist’s job, which is too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: The six steps of term research (discuss with the client, check the concept, consult a specialist, research the solution, check the solution, present it)
rows.note: Chapter 21, Step 3 has its own five-part routine for a student translator.

rows.item: Discussion with the client: concept, field, situation, source term, what has been tried; be tactful
rows.note: Reduced to “ask the client” when the meaning is unclear; the list of questions and the advice on tact were left out.

rows.item: Checking the concept in source-language dictionaries
rows.note: Chapter 3 teaches dictionary checks.

rows.item: Consulting a specialist: confirms the concept, suggests sources, clears up discrepancies
rows.note: Kept as “ask a specialist”; the specialist’s roles were not listed.

rows.item: Researching the solution: analyse the concept’s characteristics; the lighthouse rotating light (beacon); bilingual term banks and glossaries; “Can you find the Arabic?”
rows.note: Too detailed; the handbook lists its own Arabic sources in Chapter 21, Step 3.

rows.item: Checking the solution in monolingual works before giving it to the client
rows.note: Kept as advice to confirm the equivalent in a text written in Arabic; Chapter 3, Step 1 gives a similar check for dictionaries.

rows.item: Presenting the solution: justify it, name the source and the specialist, or suggest by analogy
rows.note: Client reporting is too advanced; the source column in the term list (Chapter 21, Step 4) lets readers record where they checked.

rows.item: Why consult general works before specialised ones: quicker, an overview, but less technical detail
rows.note: The reasons were left out; Chapter 21, Step 3 keeps only the advice to start with a short introduction.

rows.item: Exercise slides (headings only in the notes)
rows.note: No content to use; the handbook has its own Try it questions.

source: Terminology class notes: Comparative Terminology, Week 6 [Shaikhah Alkhaledi]

rows.item: Introduction: bilingual research must compare source and target terms to see whether they are equivalent
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Full equivalence: same meaning and use in a field (black out and {{انقطاع الكهرباء}})
rows.note: Chapter 10 teaches equivalence in a simpler way (formal, functional and ideational).

rows.item: Partial equivalence: differences in meaning (general versus specific; shifts) and in use (register, region, age, frequency)
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Limits of partial equivalence: coffee table; a language community’s right to its own terms
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Textual match: matching contexts and illustrations on a bilingual record prove that two terms are equivalent
rows.note: Record formats and proof of equivalence are too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Exercise: two Apple Watch support pages, one English and one Arabic
rows.note: Class exercise based on web pages; not suited to print.

source: Terminology class notes: Terminological Records, Week 8 [Shaikhah Alkhaledi]

rows.item: Why records: published glossaries are fixed, but a record is easy to change and update
rows.note: Record keeping is too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: What a terminology record is; sequential and condensed formats; manual and computerised records
rows.note: Record formats are too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: The 11 fields of a monolingual record
rows.note: Too detailed; Chapter 21, Step 4 names only the term, definition, field, source and date of a termbase entry.

rows.item: Entry field rules: lower case, singular nouns, infinitive verbs, synonyms after a semicolon
rows.note: Too detailed for beginners.

rows.item: Source field: a code, with the full reference on a separate record
rows.note: Reduced to one column for the source of each term in the term list; codes and separate source records were left out.

rows.item: Date of publication; volume, issue and page number
rows.note: Too detailed for beginners.

rows.item: Grammatical labels (cross over; ratings), usage and semantic labels, context, fields, author and date, access keys
rows.note: Too detailed for beginners.

rows.item: Bilingual records: 18 fields, the target fields repeating the source fields
rows.note: Too detailed for beginners.

rows.item: Key points: synonyms on separate cross-referenced records; shortening contexts with an ellipsis; source codes; label abbreviations
rows.note: Too detailed for beginners.

source: Terminology class notes: Terminological Analysis, Week 6 [Shaikhah Alkhaledi]

rows.item: Introduction: analysis identifies terms and studies their contexts; five factors for identifying terms
rows.note: Too advanced for beginners.

rows.item: Determinant and determinatum: desktop publishing, subliminal advertising, film editing; charitable institution versus charitable man; inessential (intricate technology product, initial verification technique) and essential (bait-and-switch advertising, advocacy advertising) determinants
rows.note: Too technical for beginners.

rows.item: Degree of lexicalisation: security of networks, network security and security as forms of one term
rows.note: Only network security is kept, as an example of a several-word term translated as one unit; lexicalisation is not explained.

rows.item: Classification of concepts: unsystematic, systematic, cluster, area and stratified sampling
rows.note: Too technical for beginners.

rows.item: Collocations as terms: acknowledge receipt of a message, clear a buffer, formulate a query
rows.note: Chapter 8 teaches collocation on its own.

rows.item: Typographic clues to terms: bold, italics, quotation marks, underlining
rows.note: Too detailed for beginners.

rows.item: Contextual analysis: semantic features, choosing a context, and defining, explanatory and associative contexts
rows.note: Too technical for beginners.

rows.item: Exercise: find five terminology units in a text on nuclear weapons, choose contexts, and find Arabic equivalents
rows.note: Class exercise based on a separate text.

rows.item: Opening aim: a handbook that is practical, engaging and useful for undergraduates, lasting rather than academic or dry; the sections below offered as ideas to discuss, not a fixed framework
rows.note: Kept as the aim of a plain, practical guide for beginners; the aim of lasting relevance is not stated in the book.

rows.item: Breaking the Literal Trap: real legal, technical and news examples of moving beyond word-for-word translation
rows.where: Start here; Chapter 1, Step 1; Chapter 11, Steps 1 to 4; Chapter 19, Steps 2 and 3
rows.note: Not a separate section; the news, legal and technical examples sit in the chapters they illustrate.

rows.item: The Terminology Guide: established Arabic equivalents, Arabization ({{تعريب}}) and transliteration ({{نقحرة}})
rows.where: Chapter 21, Step 3; Chapter 17, Step 2; Chapter 16, Steps 1 and 2
rows.note: Covered as a chapter on terms; the book uses “Arabicisation” ({{التعريب}}) and {{النقل الصوتي}}, not {{نقحرة}}.

rows.item: Quick-Reference Genre Checklists: step-by-step checklists for each text type
rows.where: Chapter 19, Step 2; Chapter 18, Step 4; Translation quality checklist (end of Part 8)
rows.note: Merged into one checklist for any text, one short list of rules for each genre, and one final checklist.

rows.item: The Common Pitfalls Clinic: common grammar, word and style mistakes with better versions
rows.note: Shown as weak version then better version, for both directions, inside the revision chapter rather than as a separate clinic.

rows.item: The Translation Brief (Skopos) Blueprint: before writing, ask who the client is, what the communicative purpose (Skopos) is, and who the target audience is
rows.where: Chapter 2 (Before you start: ask three questions); Chapter 26, Step 3
rows.note: Kept as three questions that make the translation brief; the word Skopos appears only in Chapter 26.

rows.item: The Interlingual Risk Assessment Matrix: judging a text by the consequences of a mistake, lower-risk general prose versus higher-risk legal and technical texts
rows.note: Written as a table of risk areas with what to do; the text-type contrast is shown through the medicine leaflet and contract examples.

rows.item: The Intertextual Mapping Protocol: before translating, find real target-language parallel texts (for example a Kuwaiti or Gulf decree) for terms, phrasing, style and register
rows.where: Chapter 3, Step 1; Chapter 21, Step 3; When in doubt page; Your journey continues
rows.note: Only the habit of checking real texts in the target language is kept; the step-by-step protocol needs texts and practice.

rows.item: Corpora and Digital Tool Literacy: use parallel corpora and reliable institutional glossaries (UNTERM, legislative portals) instead of relying only on dictionaries or raw machine translation
rows.where: Chapter 3, Step 3; Chapter 21, Step 3; Chapter 22, Step 5
rows.note: UNTERM and Arabterm are recommended and machine output must be checked against reliable sources; corpora and legislative portals are not mentioned.

rows.item: Dynamic Syntactic Restructuring (De-Anglicizing Syntax): avoid heavy nominalisation, long chains of prepositional phrases and needless passives; rebuild English sentences as natural Arabic verbal sentences
rows.where: Chapter 4, Step 1; Chapter 5, Step 2; Chapter 23, Step 2
rows.note: Partly covered, not as a module: verb-first sentences, noun to verb, and copying the English passive; prepositional chains are not covered.

rows.item: The Pragmatic Shift and Cultural Implicature Clinic: when a literal rendering fails, for English idioms and polite expressions, and keeping the interpersonal function
rows.where: Chapter 6, Step 2; Chapter 9; Chapter 15, Steps 1 and 4
rows.note: Partly covered through speaker meaning, idioms and set polite phrases; there is no separate clinic and the word implicature is not used.

rows.item: The “Invisible Translator” Ethical Audit: a reflective checklist on cultural assumptions, source-text bias, institutional expectations and neutrality
rows.note: Needs reflection and practice, and suits the website or a later edition; Chapter 20 and Chapter 22, Step 6 touch on point of view and responsibility.

rows.item: Companion website, the reasoning: the printed book carries what lasts and the website what moves; a lean first edition; corrections and growth without a new print run; future team members contribute; the website to be the final step, still a proposal
rows.note: This is the case for the website, not reader content; the book carries only the code and address.

rows.item: Companion website, Access: a QR code at the end of the handbook, one scan into the current version
rows.where: Back cover (Midnight and Light editions); last page of the book; Your journey continues
rows.note: Kept as a QR code and the address translators-guild.vercel.app, with an invitation to visit the team’s website.

rows.item: Companion website, The Library: current and earlier editions, corrections, a bank of practice texts across genres with model translations and commentary, a growing glossary, links to corpora and institutional glossaries
rows.note: Belongs on the website; the book has its own glossary and one practice text, Put it all together.

rows.item: Companion website, The Practice Arena: the handbook becomes something students do
rows.note: Belongs on the website; the book has Try it questions at the end of each chapter.

rows.item: Practice Arena: Text of the Week, a weekly passage; students submit a version and compare it with others and the commentary
rows.note: Needs weekly release and online submission, so it belongs on the website.

rows.item: Practice Arena: Spot the Literal Trap, several renderings of one sentence and a choice of the natural one
rows.note: Website activity; Chapter 11, Step 2 compares three versions of one sentence as a worked example.

rows.item: Practice Arena: Idiom Arena, timed rounds matching English idioms to Arabic equivalents
rows.note: Needs a timed online game; Chapter 9 lists idioms with their equivalents.

rows.item: Practice Arena: De-Anglicize It, a nominalised passive English sentence rebuilt as a natural Arabic verbal sentence
rows.note: Website activity; Chapter 4 and Chapter 23 have Try it questions on rewriting sentences.

rows.item: Practice Arena: Before and After, student translations beside polished versions, annotated
rows.note: Needs student work collected over time, so it belongs on the website.

rows.item: Practice Arena: streaks, badges and a team leaderboard
rows.note: Needs an online system, so it belongs on the website.

rows.item: Practice Arena: the Workshop Companion, a mode for Guild Season workshops
rows.note: Needs the website and live workshops.
